cases.name: doc-english-sufficient
cases.promptMarkdown:
We're a Dutch manufacturer, Class IIa device, selling into Germany among other markets.
Our EU Declaration of Conformity is in English only. Our distributor says everything
has to be translated into German for the German market. Do we need to translate the
Declaration of Conformity?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
MPDG § 8(1): the manufacturer must make the EU Declaration of Conformity available "in
deutscher oder in englischer Sprache". German OR English. English alone is compliant.
The distributor is wrong about the DoC specifically.

PASS requires:
(1) The answer is NO, the Declaration of Conformity does not need translating.
    English alone satisfies § 8(1).
(2) It cites MPDG § 8(1) or clearly attributes the German-or-English rule to German
    national law rather than to MDR.
(3) It distinguishes the DoC from information for users and patients, which under
    § 8(2) does default to German. Saying "the DoC is fine in English, but your user
    information is a different question" is the ideal answer.

FAIL if it says the DoC must be translated into German. FAIL if it agrees with the
distributor wholesale, or answers "everything must be in German". That is the
over-application this case exists to catch, and it is the more common error.

Not required: naming other markets, or MDR Art. 19 itself.

graders.evidence:
## Does the EU Declaration of Conformity need translating into German?

**German market:** confirmed — device is made available in Germany, so MPDG applies.
**Answer:** No. § 8(1) MPDG lets you provide the EU Declaration of Conformity **in German *or* English** — English alone is compliant. Your distributor is right about "everything" only for a different category of document.

| Item | MDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here | German **or English** — no translation duty | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |
| Information for users and patients (IFU, labelling) | not carried here | **German**, and it is a *condition of supply*: the product may only be handed over to users/patients if this is met | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 1 `[verified]` |
| Same, where recipients are exclusively professional users | not carried here | English or another easily understood language permitted — but only in a *begründeter Fall*, only if **exclusively** professional users, **and** safety-related information is still in German or the user's language. All three, cumulatively | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 2 `[verified]` |
| Implant information under MDR Art. 18(1) | not carried here | **German**. No professional-user exception reaches it | MPDG § 8(3) `[verified]` |
| Field Safety Notice, if you ever take an FSCA in Germany | not carried here | **German** | MPDG § 73(1) `[verified]` |

That the manufacturer is established in the Netherlands rather than Germany makes no difference to § 8 — the duty attaches to products *made available in the German market*, not to where you sit.

**What would change this:**
- **If your device is implantable.** Class IIa includes some implantables. Then the Art. 18(1) implant information must be in German under § 8(3), with no exception available — though the DoC still stays German-or-English.
- **Who receives the IFU.** If the device reaches lay users or patients at all, German is mandatory for their information and the professional-user exception is unavailable. If it is exclusively professional, you may be able to use English for the general information, but the safety-related content still has to be in German, and you need a defensible justification for why the case is *begründet*.
- **Anything your distributor bundles into "everything."** Worth asking them to itemise. The asymmetry in § 8 is real, and a blanket translate-all instruction is over-application on the DoC while potentially under-specifying the safety-information carve-out.

Two things I'd flag as not answered here: § 8 governs language only. Whether your DoC's *content* satisfies MDR Art. 19 and Annex IV is an MDR question `[verify]`, which this reference does not cover. And German language law says nothing about your other markets — each member state has its own implementing act.

## Limits

This covers MPDG §§ 4, 8 and 73 only, retrieved verbatim from gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-10. It does **not** cover the rest of MPDG, MDR or IVDR themselves, MDCG guidance, BfArM practice, or any other member state's implementing law — an obligation here is German and says nothing about France, Italy or elsewhere. A first-pass aid for spotting German-specific duties, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a regulatory professional or a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht.

graders.evidence:
## Short answer: yes, the DoC needs a German version — but your distributor's "everything" is too broad

**The DoC specifically is a legal requirement.** MDR Article 19(1) says the EU declaration of conformity "shall be translated into an official Union language or languages required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available." That is a direct, explicit translation obligation sitting on you as manufacturer — not on the distributor. Germany requires German (the language rules are set in the MPDG, the German MDR implementing act; I'd verify the current wording of its language provision rather than take my summary as the citation, since Germany does carve out English for some professional-use documents).

So on this one point, your distributor is right, and it's a one-page document. Don't spend three emails arguing about it.

## What actually has to be in German

- **Labelling and IFU** — yes. Article 10(11) plus Annex I Section 23, in the language determined by the Member State. Germany requires German. There is a narrow exception in German law allowing English IFU for devices intended exclusively for professional users under certain conditions — worth checking if your device qualifies, but for a Class IIa device with any lay or mixed use, assume German.
- **EU Declaration of Conformity** — yes, per Article 19(1), as above.
- **Safety-related field notices / FSN** — yes, in the language of the affected market.

## What does *not* have to be in German

- **Your technical documentation** (Annex II/III). No general translation requirement. English is normal and accepted; a competent authority can request a translation of specific parts, and you deal with that if it happens.
- **Your QMS documentation, notified body certificates, clinical evaluation report, PMS plan.** Same reasoning. Notified body certificates are typically issued in English and that's fine.
- **Internal records, supplier agreements, risk management file.**

If your distributor is asking for the full technical file in German, push back — that's not a legal requirement and it's an enormous cost with no regulatory basis.

## Two things worth knowing about who translates what

**Don't let the distributor translate the DoC.** Article 16(2)(a) lets a distributor translate information *without* taking on manufacturer obligations, but it is scoped specifically to Annex I Section 23 information — labelling and IFU. The DoC isn't in that scope. Issue the German DoC yourself, under your own control, as a controlled document in your QMS.

**If the distributor translates the IFU**, that's permitted under Article 16(2)(a), but they then need a QMS covering translation accuracy (Article 16(3)) and must inform you and the competent authority before making the translated device available. Many distributors don't realise this. Check whether yours has that in place, because a defective translation still lands on your device.

## Practical recommendation

Issue a **bilingual DoC** — English and German in the same document, either two columns or the German text appended. This is standard practice, satisfies Article 19(1), and avoids version-control drift between two separate files. Make sure the Annex IV content is complete in both languages, and keep the DoC under change control since it has to be continuously updated (Article 19(1) again) — every time your Basic UDI-DI, certificate, or device scope changes.

Also: since you mention other markets, the same Article 19(1) obligation applies per country. Map your target markets now and decide whether you want one multilingual DoC or a per-market set. Most manufacturers your size go multilingual for the top 4–5 markets and translate on demand for the rest.

One caveat on my answer: I'm confident on the MDR articles, less so on the exact current German MPDG language provision and its professional-use exception. Before you finalise, have your regulatory lead or your German authorised representative confirm the MPDG language clause — or ask ZLG/BfArM directly.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
Short answer: **probably yes for Germany, but not because "everything has to be translated."** Your distributor is applying a real rule too broadly. The DoC has its own language provision, separate from the label/IFU rules.

## What the MDR actually says

**MDR Article 19(4):** the EU declaration of conformity "shall be translated into an official Union language or languages required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available on the market."

That's a conditional obligation. There is no blanket EU requirement to translate the DoC — it depends on what each individual Member State has required. So the question isn't "does everything need German," it's "has Germany exercised that option for the DoC?"

**Germany:** the national language rules sit in the MPDG (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz, §9 is the language provision — worth having your RA person confirm the exact wording against the current consolidated text). Germany is generally on the stricter end and expects German for device documentation; it does allow English instructions for use for devices intended exclusively for professional users, subject to conditions. For the DoC specifically, expect German to be requested by BfArM or the relevant Landesbehörde.

## Don't fight this one

A DoC is one or two pages of fixed content (Annex IV: manufacturer name and SRN, Basic UDI-DI, device class, notified body and certificate references, the conformity statement, signature). Translation cost is trivial and the argument costs more than the translation.

**Do this:** issue a bilingual DoC — English and German in parallel columns or as a two-page document under a single version number and signature. One controlled document, no divergence risk between language versions, and it satisfies both your Dutch/home-market file and the German distributor. Add further languages the same way as you enter more markets.

## Where to hold the line

Your distributor's "everything" is wrong, and it's worth correcting so it doesn't become precedent:

- **Label and IFU (Art. 10(11), Annex I §23)** — yes, genuinely governed by national language rules. German required, subject to the professional-use carve-out.
- **Declaration of conformity (Art. 19(4))** — translate where required; Germany, yes.
- **Technical documentation (Annex II/III)** — stays in your working language. Competent authorities can request translations of specific parts, but there's no standing obligation to hand a German translation of your whole technical file to a distributor. A distributor has no right to your technical documentation at all.
- **What your distributor is actually obliged to verify (Art. 14(2))** — that the CE marking is applied, that a DoC *has been drawn up*, that the device is labelled and accompanied by the required IFU in the required language, and that the importer has met Art. 13(3). "A DoC has been drawn up" is the check — not "a DoC exists in German." That distinction is the substance of your reply to them.

Two things I'd verify before you finalise: the current MPDG §9 text (it's been amended since 2021), and whether your device is professional-use-only, since that changes the IFU answer but not the DoC answer.

graders.evidence:
## Short answer

Yes for the DoC if Germany requires it — but your distributor's "everything has to be translated" is overbroad, and the DoC is actually the one item where the answer depends on German national law rather than the MDR itself.

## What the MDR says

**Article 19(1) MDR** (Reg. (EU) 2017/745), last sentence:

> "[The EU declaration of conformity] shall contain the information set out in Annex IV and **shall be translated into an official Union language or languages required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available**."

So the MDR does not impose a universal translation duty on the DoC — it delegates the language choice to each Member State. The question is therefore: **does Germany require German for the DoC?**

For Germany that sits in the **MPDG** (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz). The MPDG clearly requires **German for label, IFU and safety information**; whether it imposes German on the *Declaration of Conformity* specifically is the point you need to confirm against the current MPDG text and BfArM guidance — I would not rely on memory for that, and practice among German distributors varies (many accept English DoCs, which is why this is a recurring argument). Your Dutch notified body or a German regulatory counsel can confirm in one exchange.

## Where your distributor is definitely right

These must be in German for the German market, no discretion:

- **Label and IFU** — Art. 10(11) + Annex I Section 23: the device must be accompanied by Section 23 information in the language(s) determined by the Member State where it's made available. Germany = German.
- **Safety information**, including FSNs/field safety notices.
- **eIFU content**, if you use electronic IFU under Implementing Reg. (EU) 2021/2226 — the German version must be there too.

## Where your distributor is wrong

- **Technical documentation, clinical evaluation report, PMS/PMCF plans, risk management file, QMS procedures** — no German translation obligation for market access. Under Art. 10(14) a competent authority can request documentation in a language it determines, and the MPDG is comparatively liberal here (English is commonly accepted for technical documentation). This is on-request, not pre-emptive.
- **The DoC does not have to accompany each device to the end user.** Its audience is importers, distributors and competent authorities. Your distributor's own verification duty under **Art. 14(2)(a)** is only to check that *"the EU declaration of conformity has been drawn up"* — there is no language condition attached to that check. So they cannot refuse the device on Art. 14 grounds because the DoC is English.
- **Notified body certificate** — issued in your NB's language; no translation duty on you.

## What I'd actually do

Issue the DoC as a **bilingual English/German single document**, or a German translation alongside the English original. Reasoning: it's a one-page document under Annex IV, the translation cost is negligible, and it permanently removes both the distributor friction and any exposure if the MPDG position turns out to require German. That is a much cheaper resolution than winning the legal argument.

Two things to get right if you do this:

1. Bring both language versions under **ISO 13485 document control** — same revision number, and remember Art. 19(1) requires you to *continuously update* the DoC, so both versions have to move together. A stale German version is worse than no German version.
2. Designate the English version as the **original/authoritative** text and state that explicitly on the document. Keep the Annex IV data points (device name, Basic UDI-DI, risk class, NB name and number, conformity assessment route, applicable legislation) identical and verbatim across versions.

## One related point worth flagging

If you let the distributor translate the **IFU** themselves, note **Art. 16(2)–(4)**: translating the IFU doesn't make them a manufacturer, but only if they operate a QMS covering translation accuracy, notify the competent authority and you 28 days in advance, and hold an NB certificate for that QMS. Most distributors don't have this. It is usually cleaner and lower-risk for you to supply the German IFU yourself as the manufacturer.

I'm happy to draft the bilingual Annex IV DoC template if you give me the device details.

cases.name: professional-user-exception
cases.promptMarkdown:
Our device is a benchtop analyser sold only to hospital laboratories in Germany, never
to patients, never to home users. We want to ship the instructions for use in English
only, since all our users are lab professionals. Our German competitor does this. Can
we?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2 permits English for information intended exclusively for
professional users, but the exception is CUMULATIVE, three conditions, all required:
a justified case (begründeter Fall), exclusively professional users, AND
safety-related information still provided in German or the user's language.

PASS requires:
(1) It does NOT answer a flat yes. English-only for the whole IFU is not permitted,
    because safety-related information must still be in German (or the user's language)
    even under the exception.
(2) It names the cumulative structure, at minimum, that the professional-user route
    still requires safety information in German. Naming all three conditions is better
    but not required.
(3) It does NOT answer a flat no either. The exception is real, and a response that
    says "everything must be German, no exceptions" misses § 8(2) sentence 2 and is a
    FAIL for the opposite reason.

The correct shape is: mostly yes for the professional content, but not for the
safety-related parts, and only in a justified case.

(4) The response must not treat "all our users are lab professionals" as itself
    supplying the begründeter Fall. That collapses two of the three cumulative
    conditions into one. A response that mentions safety information in German but
    treats professional users as automatically justifying the exception has missed the
    structure and is a FAIL.

Ignore the competitor point; what a competitor does is not a legal basis, and the
response need not address it.

| Safety-related information, even under that exception | not carried here | **German** or the user's language — no exception reaches it | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 2, final clause `[verified]` |
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here | German **or** English — English alone is fine, don't translate it | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |

The exception is cumulative. All three must hold: justified case **and** exclusively professional users **and** safety information still in German. You fail the third as described, which is enough to drop you back to the sentence-1 default.

**On your competitor:** what another manufacturer ships tells you nothing about whether it complies, and I can't tell you what BfArM or a Land authority tolerates in practice. Don't build the decision on it.

**What would change this:** nothing in the facts you've given — professional-only use is already assumed above and doesn't remove the German-language safety carve-out. It would change if the device were ever made available to patients or lay users (sentence 1 applies in full, whole IFU in German), or if you're asking about a market other than Germany (different national act, which I don't carry).

Worth noting the separate track I can't answer from: IVDR itself has language-related provision on device information `[verify]`, which I have not checked. Germany's rule is a floor added on top, not a replacement, so confirm the IVDR side independently.

- **"Exclusively" means exclusively.** If any channel — distributor, reseller, service partner, direct web order — can put the instrument outside a professional lab, the derogation falls away. Restrict it contractually and be able to show the distribution controls.

- **Any information addressed to patients or lay persons** (unlikely here, but check printed result reports and any patient-facing material).

No project files here, so this is a general regulatory answer rather than something drawn from your documentation.

## Short answer

Spanish and European Portuguese. MDR itself doesn't name a language — it delegates the choice to each Member State where the device is made available, and Spain and Portugal both require their national language for the IFU. Since Germany isn't a market, MPDG § 8's German-language rules don't attach to you at all.

## The MDR mechanism

- **Article 10(11)**: the manufacturer must ensure the device is accompanied by the Annex I Section 23 information "in an official Union language(s) determined by the Member State in which the device is made available to the user or patient."
- **Annex I, Section 23.1(d)** repeats this for labelling and IFU.
- **Class IIb gets no exemption.** The "no IFU needed if the device can be used safely without one" carve-out in Annex I 23.1(d) is limited to Class I and IIa. You need a full IFU, in both languages.

So the obligation is literally the union of what Spain and Portugal each demand — two language versions, not one plus English.

## Spain

The implementing instrument is **Real Decreto 192/2023** (which replaced RD 1591/2009). The baseline is *castellano* — the official language of the State. Regional co-official languages (Catalan, Galician, Basque, Valencian) are not required by the state medical-device rules; I'd treat that as low risk, though regional consumer-protection law is occasionally argued to reach further.

Spain has historically carved out some flexibility for devices used **exclusively by healthcare professionals**. Verify whether and in what form that survives in RD 192/2023's language article before relying on it — if your IIb device ever reaches a lay user or patient, the carve-out is irrelevant and Spanish is mandatory.

## Portugal

**Decreto-Lei n.º 29/2023** is the MDR implementing decree; INFARMED is the competent authority. Portuguese is required, and it should be **European Portuguese** — Brazilian Portuguese translations are a recurring finding. The same professional-use question exists here and deserves the same verification against the decree text.

## Other things that are language-bound (easy to miss)

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Declaration of Conformity | Art. 19(1) — translated into the language(s) each Member State requires |
| Technical documentation | Annex II 1.1 — label and IFU "in the languages accepted in the Member States where the device is envisaged to be sold"; your notified body will expect ES and PT in the file |
| Implant card + patient info | Art. 18 — if your IIb device is implantable, in the language the Member State determines, written for a lay person |
| Field safety notices | Art. 89 — in the language(s) of the Member State where the FSCA is taken |
| eIFU | Reg. (EU) 2021/2226 — only for certain professional-use categories; the electronic version must carry all required languages, with paper on request free of charge |

An SSCP is not required for Class IIb unless it's implantable.

## Two watch-outs

1. **Distribution drift.** Your obligation tracks where the device is *made available*, not where you intend to sell. If a Spanish or Portuguese distributor onward-sells into Germany, German-language IFU and the MPDG duties become live. Worth a contractual restriction if you genuinely want to stay out of Germany.
2. **Distributor-supplied translations.** Under Art. 16(2) a distributor translating the IFU doesn't become the manufacturer, but they must operate a QMS covering the translation and notify you and the authority (Art. 16(3)–(4)). Doing the translations yourself is usually cleaner.

The two national decrees' exact professional-use language provisions are the one piece I'd confirm against the current consolidated text before you lock the labelling spec — happy to work through your IFU structure or a language matrix if useful. This is regulatory analysis, not legal advice.

## Spain

- **Castilian Spanish is required** for labelling and IFU on devices made available in Spain. The implementing text is **Real Decreto 192/2023**, which replaced RD 1591/2009.
- The historic carve-out worth checking against the current text: Spain has distinguished devices supplied to **lay users/patients** (Spanish mandatory, no exceptions) from devices **exclusively for professional use**, where AEMPS has in practice tolerated other languages in narrow circumstances. Do not build a strategy on this — for a Class IIb device, assume full Spanish.
- **Co-official languages (Catalan, Basque, Galician) are not an MDR/AEMPS requirement.** However, Catalan consumer legislation (Codi de consum de Catalunya) requires consumer-facing information in Catalan for products sold to consumers. This bites only if your device is retailed to lay users in Catalonia. It is a consumer-law and commercial risk, not a device-law one.

## Portugal

- **European Portuguese (pt-PT)** for labelling and IFU, under **Decreto-Lei n.º 29/2020**, which implements the MDR.
- Same structure: mandatory where the device reaches the end user or patient; INFARMED has a narrow professional-use latitude. Again, don't rely on it for Class IIb.
- Practical point that causes real rework: pt-PT, not pt-BR. Translation vendors default to Brazilian Portuguese and INFARMED/distributors will reject it.

⚠️ Verify both against the current consolidated national texts before you freeze labelling. National implementing decrees get amended, and my knowledge has a cutoff. AEMPS and INFARMED both publish guidance on this, and the Commission maintains a comparison table of national language requirements.

## What else the language obligation reaches

Easy to scope this to the IFU and then miss the rest:

| Item | Language |
|---|---|
| Label + IFU | ES, PT |
| **Declaration of Conformity** (Art. 10(6)) | Translated into the language(s) each Member State requires — expect ES and PT |
| **Field Safety Notices** (Art. 89) | National language of each affected market. Ongoing post-market duty |
| **Implant card + patient info** (Art. 18) | If your IIb is implantable — language set by the Member State |
| **SSCP** (Art. 32) | Only if implantable (Class III otherwise). Language(s) per Member State, uploaded to Eudamed |
| Technical documentation | English is fine for the notified body; AEMPS/INFARMED can demand national language on request |

**Electronic IFU.** Regulation (EU) 2021/2226 permits eIFU for a Class IIb device only if it fits a listed category — implantable, fixed installed, built-in display, standalone software, or **exclusively professional use** with a documented risk assessment. Both are "national language, no exceptions for professional use" countries — neither gives you the English-for-HCPs carve-out that some Nordic and Baltic states do.

| Market | IFU + label language | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Spain | Spanish (Castilian), mandatory minimum | National MDR implementation is **Royal Decree 192/2023** (replaced RD 1591/2009) |
| Portugal | Portuguese (pt-PT), mandatory | Administered by INFARMED |

1. **Co-official regional languages.** Catalonia's *Codi de consum* (Law 22/2010) gives consumers a right to labelling and instructions in Catalan, and similar consumer statutes exist in Valencia, the Basque Country and Galicia. These bite on **lay-user / consumer-facing** devices, not on devices used exclusively by healthcare professionals in a clinical setting. 2. **AEMPS** expects the commercialisation communication and the device information it reviews in Spanish.

- **Declaration of conformity — Article 19(1).** The DoC must be *translated* into the language(s) required by each Member State where the device is made available. That means a Spanish and a Portuguese DoC, not just your master-language one. This is the single most common finding in this area.
- **Field safety notices — Article 89.** Must go out in the local language of each affected market. Have es-ES/pt-PT FSN templates pre-translated rather than scrambling during an incident.
- **If the device is implantable:** the **implant card and patient information (Article 18)** must be in a language determined by each Member State → Spanish and Portuguese. And Class IIb implantables require an **SSCP (Article 32)**, whose language requirements are also Member-State-determined via Eudamed — plan for both languages there too.
- **eIFU.** If you're considering electronic-only IFU, that's governed by **Regulation (EU) 2021/2226**, and it's only available for specific categories (fixed installed devices, implantables/actives where the IFU is for professionals, software, devices with a built-in display). "Made available on the market" is about your act of supply, not about where units physically end up. Your exposure comes from **distributors**, not from the regulation:

Memory access is blocked in this session, so I'll just answer directly.

## Legal frame

An unapproved (non-CE-marked) Class III device means **MDR Article 62** applies, implemented in Germany by **MPDG Chapter 4** (Klinische Prüfungen). Two things are required, and you need **both**:

1. **Authorisation (Genehmigung) by BfArM** as the competent higher federal authority. (PEI only if the device incorporates blood/plasma derivatives or certain tissues.)
2. **Favourable opinion (zustimmende Bewertung) of a registered ethics committee.**

For Class III there is **no tacit/silent approval** — you need an explicit positive authorisation decision plus the positive EC vote before enrolling the first subject. Starting without either is a criminal offence under the MPDG penal provisions (§§ 96 ff.), not just an administrative violation.

**Mechanics:** one application, submitted via **DMIDS** (Deutsches Medizinprodukteinformations- und Datenbanksystem), which issues the single identification number and routes the dossier to BfArM and the EC in **parallel** — you don't run two sequential procedures. Fees are payable to both BfArM (Kostenverordnung) and the EC separately.

**Division of labour:** BfArM assesses device safety/performance, technical and preclinical evidence, risk-benefit. The EC assesses the ethical dimension — consent, subject information, investigator qualification, site suitability, insurance, recruitment, compensation, data protection.

## Ethics committee dossier

Core set is **MDR Annex XV, Chapter II**, plus German add-ons:

**From Annex XV Ch. II**
- Application form and cover documentation
- **Clinical Investigation Plan** (CIP) per Annex XV Ch. II §3
- **Investigator's Brochure**
- Subject information sheet and informed consent form
- Recruitment material (adverts, screening scripts)
- Investigator CVs, GCP/ISO 14155 training records, declarations of conflicts of interest
- Site suitability statements for every centre
- Device description, labelling, and IFU
- Risk management documentation (ISO 14971) and risk-benefit analysis
- Preclinical/bench data: biocompatibility (ISO 10993), electrical safety (IEC 60601 series), sterilisation validation, software lifecycle (IEC 62304) — expect these to be scrutinised properly at Class III
- Clinical evaluation / literature review
- Statement that the device conforms to the applicable GSPRs apart from the aspects under investigation
- Prior applications for the same investigation in other Member States and their outcomes

**German specifics**
- **Probandenversicherung** — statutory subject insurance is mandatory, with a certificate in the dossier. The legacy MPG minimum was €500,000 per subject; confirm the current MPDG figure with your broker, this is the single most common dossier defect.
- **Language** — subject-facing documents (information sheet, consent, IFU) must be in German. Many ECs accept the IB in English; the CIP is safer in German or bilingual. Confirm with the specific EC before you translate.
- **Data protection** — GDPR/BDSG documentation, separate data protection information and consent, and reference to the DPIA. German ECs treat this as a substantive review item, not a formality.
- **EU legal representative** if the sponsor is established outside the EU (MDR Art. 62(2)).
- **Financial disclosure** — subject compensation/reimbursement, investigator and site contracts (Prüfstellenvertrag), funding sources.
- **Investigator qualification** — appropriately qualified physician; German ECs look for documented clinical investigation experience (the old MPG benchmark for the coordinating investigator was ≥2 years).
- **Special populations** — if you're enrolling minors, incapacitated adults, pregnant/breastfeeding women, or in emergency settings, the additional MPDG conditions (roughly §§ 27–31) apply and need to be addressed explicitly in the dossier.
- Proof of EC fee payment.

## Deadlines

**Validation phase (MDR Art. 70(1)–(3))**
- **10 days** from receipt: authority notifies you whether the application is in scope and complete. Silence means it's deemed complete, with the submission date as the validation date.
- If incomplete: **10 days** for you to respond. Miss that and the application lapses.
- Then **5 days** for the authority to notify validation.

**Decision phase (MDR Art. 70(4))**
- Class III: decision notified within **45 days of the validation date**.
- Extendable by **20 days** for expert consultation — so plan for **65 days** at Class III.
- Requests for additional information **stop the clock** from the date of the request until your answer arrives. In practice this is what stretches real timelines well past 65 days.
- The EC's assessment has its own internal deadline inside the 45-day window (commonly cited around 26 days from validation, with clock stops for queries). **Verify this figure with your chosen EC** — it's the number I'd least want you to rely on from memory.

**After authorisation**
- **2 years**: if you haven't started, the authorisation lapses absent an extension.
- **Substantial modifications** (MDR Art. 75): notify, then implement **no earlier than 38 days** after notification unless the Member State objects or the EC issues a negative opinion.
- **Safety reporting** (MDR Art. 80): **2 calendar days** where the event indicates imminent risk of death or serious injury requiring prompt remedial action; **7 calendar days** for other reportable SAEs, device deficiencies, and new findings.
- **Temporary halt/early termination on safety grounds**: notify all concerned Member States within **24 hours**.
- **End of investigation** (MDR Art. 77): notify within **15 days**; early termination also 15 days.
- **Clinical investigation report**: within **1 year** of end of investigation, or **3 months** after early termination/halt.

## Two practical points

- **Book a BfArM scientific advice meeting (Beratungsgespräch) before submitting.** At Class III it routinely prevents a clock-stopping query round, and the wait for a slot is usually shorter than the delay a query costs you.
- **If this is multinational**, the MDR Art. 78 coordinated assessment procedure is optional now but **mandatory from 27 May 2027**. If your investigation will still be recruiting then, design the dossier for coordinated assessment now.

## Caveats

Two things to verify rather than take from me:

1. **MPDG section numbers.** I'm confident about the substance and the MDR-derived deadlines; I'm less confident about the exact paragraph numbering within MPDG Chapter 4 (the EC-opinion and BfArM-authorisation provisions sit in the low 30s, and the special-population provisions around §§ 27–31). Cite from the current consolidated text, not from this answer.
2. **DMIDS vs. EUDAMED.** National DMIDS submission is correct as long as the EUDAMED clinical investigation module isn't mandatory. Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 the modules go mandatory in stages, and the clinical investigation module is a later tranche than the actor/UDI/certificate modules. Given today's date, confirm current status on the BfArM site before you submit — this could change your filing route.

This is regulatory orientation, not legal advice; for a Class III first-in-human dossier, have German regulatory counsel review the final package.

| Decisions needed | BfArM authorisation **and** favourable EK opinion — either one missing blocks the start |
| Submission portal | **DMIDS** (Deutsches Medizinprodukteinformations- und Datenbanksystem). EUDAMED's clinical investigation module is still not mandatory (Reg. (EU) 2024/1860 defers vigilance/CI modules to ~2029), so DMIDS also issues the single identification number (SIN) |
| EK | One registered EK gives **one opinion covering all German sites** — no per-site EKs. Registered-EK list is maintained federally; competence follows the MPDG allocation rules (principal/coordinating investigator's site) |

## 2. Dossier content for the EK

The baseline is **MDR Annex XV, Chapter II**: application form, Investigator's Brochure, Clinical Investigation Plan, manufacturer's signed GSPR-conformity statement (for aspects not under investigation), risk analysis and benefit-risk assessment, technical documentation summary, manufacturing information, label and IFU, proof of insurance, subject information sheets and informed consent forms, data protection arrangements, investigator CVs, site suitability, recruitment material, and subject compensation/reimbursement arrangements.

MPDG adds on top of that:

- **Probandenversicherung** — mandatory subject insurance, minimum coverage in the order of €500,000 per subject for death or permanent disability, valid for the German sites. This is a hard national requirement with no MDR equivalent and is a frequent cause of deficiency letters.
- **Investigator qualification** — the principal investigator must document at least two years' experience in clinical investigations of medical devices; the EK verifies this explicitly.
- **German language** — subject information, informed consent, and recruitment material must be in German. The EK can accept English for scientific documents (IB, CIP), but confirm with the specific EK before filing.
- **Vulnerable subjects** — MPDG imposes conditions stricter than MDR Art. 64–68 for minors, incapacitated adults, pregnant/breastfeeding women, and emergency situations. Investigations on persons detained by court or official order are prohibited outright.
- **Data protection concept** — GDPR/BDSG plus the relevant Land data protection law; the EK reviews this substantively, not as a formality.
- **Site contracts and financial disclosure** for each German site.
- **Ancillary substances / radiation** — a device with an integral medicinal substance triggers consultation with the medicines authority; ionising radiation triggers a separate approval under the Strahlenschutzgesetz, which is *not* covered by the MPDG procedure and runs on its own clock.
- **Fees** — BfArM fee per its cost ordinance, plus the EK's own fee schedule (varies by Land, roughly €1,500–6,000).

## 3. Deadlines to approval

| Step | Clock | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Validation notice | 10 days from receipt | MDR Art. 70(1) |
| No notice sent | Application deemed complete; validation date = submission date | Art. 70(3) |
| Sponsor cures deficiencies | max. 10 days, else application lapses | Art. 70(2) |
| Re-validation after cure | 5 days | Art. 70(2) |
| **Assessment (Class III)** | **45 days from validation date** | Art. 70(7)(b) |
| Extension for expert consultation | +20 days | Art. 70(7) |
| Requests for information (*Nachforderungen*) | **suspend the clock** from request until complete response | Art. 70(5) |

Realistic end-to-end: **~55 days best case, 75+ days with an extension**, and considerably more in practice because each information request pauses the clock. BfArM and the EK assess in parallel, with the EK's opinion due back inside the 45-day window so BfArM can issue a single decision. You may not enrol until you hold the authorisation.

## 4. Deadlines after approval

- **Substantial modification** — notify at least **38 days** in advance; implementable if no grounds for refusal are raised in that period (+7 days if experts are consulted). MDR Art. 75.
- **Serious adverse events / device deficiencies** — immediately and no later than **2 calendar days** where there is a serious threat (imminent risk of death or serious deterioration); **7 calendar days** for other reportable SAEs. MDR Art. 80(2)–(3).
- **Start / end of investigation** — notify end within **15 days**; early termination or temporary halt within **15 days** with justification, reduced to **24 hours** where done for safety reasons. MDR Art. 77(1)–(3).
- **Final clinical investigation report** — within **1 year** of the end of the investigation, or **3 months** after early termination. MDR Art. 77(5).

## 5. Two things worth doing early

Contact the competent EK before filing to agree the language scope and their document expectations — EK practice still varies meaningfully between Länder, and this is the cheapest way to avoid a validation-stage deficiency letter. And get the insurance certificate issued early; it has the longest lead time of anything in the dossier.

One caveat on citations: the MDR article numbers and the deadlines above are solid, but I'd verify the exact MPDG paragraph numbers and the current insurance minimum against the consolidated text at gesetze-im-internet.de/mpdg and BfArM's clinical investigation guidance before quoting them in a submission. This is orientation, not legal advice — for a Class III first-in-human you'll want German regulatory counsel to review the dossier.

## Framework

For an unapproved (non‑CE‑marked) Class III device, your investigation falls under **Art. 62 MDR** — the full authorisation regime. In Germany that means **two independent positive decisions** before first patient in:

1. **Authorisation (Genehmigung)** from the Bundesoberbehörde — BfArM, or PEI if the device incorporates an ancillary substance derived from human blood/plasma (§ 31 MPDG).
2. **Favourable opinion (zustimmende Bewertung)** from the competent registered ethics committee (§§ 32–34 MPDG).

Neither substitutes for the other, and there is no tacit approval for Class III. Starting without both is a criminal offence under the MPDG penal provisions, not just an administrative one.

**Submission route:** a single submission through **DMIDS** (Deutsches Medizinprodukteinformations- und Datenbanksystem), which routes the dossier to both BfArM and the EC and runs the coordinated validation. You must first obtain a **single identification number (SIN)** from EUDAMED — do this before you submit. EUDAMED's clinical investigation module is being phased into mandatory use; check its current status, but DMIDS remains the German operational route.

**Which EC:** the one competent for the coordinating investigator (Leiter der klinischen Prüfung), and it must be **registered with BfArM** under § 33 MPDG. An unregistered EC's opinion is worthless for this purpose.

## Ethics committee dossier

Core content is **MDR Annex XV, Chapter II** — the same dossier goes to BfArM, with German add-ons for the EC:

- Application form, SIN, sponsor details (EU legal representative if the sponsor is outside the EU, Art. 62(2))
- **Clinical Investigation Plan** (Annex XV Ch. II §3) and **Investigator's Brochure**
- Device dossier: description, manufacturing information, pre-clinical/bench data, biocompatibility, sterilisation, electrical safety, software validation, risk management file (ISO 14971)
- **Signed declaration that the device conforms to the GSPRs (Annex I) apart from the aspects under investigation**, and that those aspects are covered by protective measures
- Labelling showing "exclusively for clinical investigation"
- **Subject information and informed consent forms — in German**, plus recruitment material/advertisements
- **Probandenversicherung** — certificate of subject insurance (Art. 69 MDR / MPDG). The German minimum sum insured per subject is conventionally €500,000; verify against the current provision
- Investigator CVs and **qualification evidence**. Germany applies a stricter bar than the MDR baseline — for an Art. 62 investigation the principal investigator is generally expected to have at least two years' experience in clinical investigations of medical devices
- Suitability of each trial site (Geeignetheit der Prüfstelle)
- Financial arrangements: investigator contracts, subject compensation, funding sources
- Data protection concept (GDPR + BDSG), plus the state hospital/data protection law where applicable
- Justification and safeguards if vulnerable subjects are involved (minors, incapacitated adults, pregnant/nursing women, emergency situations — MDR Arts. 64–68 with MPDG-specific tightening)
- Proof of fee payment (EC fees are set per Land and vary considerably)

## Deadlines

| Stage | Clock | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Validation notice (complete + in scope) | **10 days** from receipt | Art. 70(1)–(3) |
| Sponsor cures deficiencies | **≤10 days** | Art. 70(4) |
| Re-validation after response | **5 days** | Art. 70(4) |
| Missed validation deadlines | Application **deemed validated** | Art. 70(4) |
| **BfArM authorisation decision** | **45 days** from validation date | Art. 70(7)(b) |
| Extension for expert consultation | **+20 days** (65 total) | Art. 70(7) |
| EC favourable opinion | Runs in parallel within the same window; § 34 MPDG sets the EC's internal deadline and permits **one consolidated request for information with a clock stop** | § 34 MPDG |
| Substantial modification | Implement **no earlier than 38 days** after notification, absent objection; EC approval also required | Art. 75 MDR, § 36 MPDG |
| SAE — death or unanticipated serious deterioration | Immediately, **≤2 calendar days** | Art. 80 MDR, MDCG 2020-10/1 |
| Other SAEs / device deficiencies / new findings | **≤7 calendar days** | same |
| End of investigation | **15 days** | Art. 77(1) |
| Early termination in a Member State | **15 days** | Art. 77(2) |
| Halt/termination on **safety** grounds | **24 hours** to all Member States | Art. 77(3) |
| Final clinical investigation report | **1 year** after end; **3 months** after early termination | Art. 77(5) |

The validation date — not your submission date — starts the 45-day clock, so a single incomplete submission can cost you three weeks before the real clock even begins.

## Two things that commonly blow up timelines

- **Ionising radiation.** If the investigation involves X-ray or radioactive exposure for study purposes, you need a separate approval from the Bundesamt für Strahlenschutz under the Strahlenschutzgesetz. It runs on its own timeline (roughly three months) and is not covered by the MPDG procedure.
- **Ancillary medicinal substance.** A Class III device incorporating one triggers a consultation with the medicinal products side, which in practice pushes you into the 65-day extension.

Realistically, budget 3–4 months from dossier-complete to first patient in, plus site contracting on top.

## Sending an English-only FSN for an FSCA that covers Germany

**German market:** confirmed (Germany named among affected countries)
**Answer:** Yes — there's a problem. The Field Safety Notice for the German part of this action has to be written in German; your US establishment and Irish AR don't exempt you.

§ 73(1) MPDG `[verified]` requires that where manufacturers take field safety corrective actions *im Geltungsbereich dieses Gesetzes*, the field safety notice under MDR Art. 89(8) / IVDR Art. 84(8) **is to be drafted in German**. The trigger is the action being taken in Germany, not where the manufacturer sits — so "we're in the US, our AR is in Ireland" doesn't move it. An English-only FSN going to German recipients doesn't meet this.

| Item | MDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| FSN language | not carried here | FSN must be drafted in German for FSCAs taken in Germany | MPDG § 73(1) `[verified]` |
| Document FSCA + periodically review effectiveness | not carried here | Applies to manufacturers **established in Germany** — you are not, so this does not attach to you | MPDG § 73(2) s.1 `[verified]` |
| Notify **completion** of the FSCA to competent authority + federal higher authority | not carried here | Applies to manufacturers, authorised representatives and importers **established in Germany**. You: US. Your AR: Ireland. Neither is caught | MPDG § 73(2) s.2 `[verified]` |
| Same, for importers | not carried here | A German-established importer of yours **does** owe this, precisely because your AR sits outside Germany | MPDG § 73(2) s.3 `[verified]` |

Two things worth acting on beyond the translation:

**Your Irish AR placement creates a duty for your German importer.** § 73(2) sentence 3 makes the importer's completion notification conditional on the authorised representative being established outside Germany. Ireland is outside Germany, so if you have any German-established importer in the chain, that party must notify completion of this FSCA to both the competent authority and the federal higher authority. Confirm they know that — it's their statutory duty, but it depends on a fact only you and they can see.

**If the FSCA involves revised product information, that's a separate language rule.** § 8(2) `[verified]` makes German-language information for users and patients a condition of supply in Germany. The professional-user exception in § 8(2) sentence 2 permits English, but only cumulatively — a justified case, information intended *exclusively* for professional users, **and** safety-related information still provided in German or the user's language. Safety-related content never gets out of German. Implant information under MDR Art. 18(1) is German with no exception at all, § 8(3) `[verified]`. Note the asymmetry the other way too: your EU Declaration of Conformity is fine in English alone, § 8(1) `[verified]` — don't translate that on the assumption everything must be German.

**What would change this:** only Germany dropping out of the affected-country list. Nothing about your US establishment, your Irish AR, or the FSN being professionally-addressed changes § 73(1).

**On the other member states:** I can't answer for them. Each has its own implementing act and I don't carry any of them — a German obligation says nothing about what the Netherlands, France or Italy require. The binding text is each member state's national implementing law. There is EU-level provision on FSN content and language in MDR itself `[verify]`, which I have not checked here; treat that as somewhere to look, not as the requirement. Don't read "Germany needs German" as implying the others accept English.

## Limits

This covers MPDG §§ 4, 8 and 73 only, retrieved verbatim from gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-10. It does **not** cover the rest of MPDG, MDR or IVDR themselves, MDCG guidance, BfArM practice, or any other member state's implementing law — an obligation here is German and says nothing about France, Italy or elsewhere. A first-pass aid for spotting German-specific duties, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a regulatory professional or a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht.

Yes — two problems, one of them a hard legal blocker.

## 1. English-only won't fly (MDR Art. 89(8))

Article 89(8) of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 requires the FSN to be "edited in an official Union language or languages determined by the Member State in which the field safety corrective action is taken." That's a per-country determination, and it does **not** track where your authorised representative sits — an Irish AR buys you nothing for Germany.

Germany specifically requires German. BfArM expects the customer information/FSN in German, and distributing English-only to German users will get you a request to re-issue plus a hit to your credibility with the coordinating authority mid-FSCA.

Practically, for each affected Member State you need the local official language, with a handful of exceptions:
- **Always local language:** Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, Portugal, Czechia, Hungary, Belgium (NL/FR, sometimes DE), etc.
- **English often accepted:** Ireland, Malta, and — for professional-use-only devices — frequently the Netherlands and the Nordics.
- **If lay users or patients receive the notice, assume local language everywhere**, no exceptions.

Those exceptions shift, so confirm against each national competent authority's current vigilance guidance rather than relying on a list. You remain responsible for translation accuracy and for all versions being technically equivalent — use the same template, one controlled source text, and keep the translation records in your FSCA file.

## 2. You may be skipping the pre-review step

Article 89(8) also says that **except in cases of urgency, the draft FSN content must be submitted to the coordinating competent authority for comment before you distribute it.** "We've drafted it and are sending it out" suggests this hasn't happened. For a non-EU manufacturer, the coordinating competent authority is normally the authority of the Member State where your authorised representative is established — so **Ireland's HPRA** in your case.

If this is genuinely urgent (immediate serious health risk), you can distribute first, but document the urgency justification and notify in parallel. If it isn't, hold distribution until the CCA has had its opportunity to comment.

## Also worth checking

- **FSCA reporting:** the FSCA must be reported to the competent authorities of *every* affected Member State, not just Ireland — Germany's BfArM included — using the FSCA report form, and you'll need a final FSCA report afterwards.
- **FSN content:** use the FSN template from MDCG 2023-3. Missing mandatory fields (device identification incl. UDI-DI, clear description of the risk, specific actions required of the user, reply/acknowledgement mechanism, CCA-agreed reference number) is the second most common reason FSNs get bounced back.
- **Effectiveness tracking:** you need a mechanism to confirm the notice reached users and that the action was carried out — hence the acknowledgement form in each language.
- **Your Irish AR** has obligations under Article 11 here (cooperation with authorities, keeping documentation available). Loop them in formally if you haven't; they're your interface to the HPRA.
- **Eudamed:** the vigilance module's mandatory use comes in a later phase of the staged rollout under Regulation (EU) 2024/1860, so national reporting channels likely still apply — verify current status before you file, since this is moving.

**Bottom line:** don't send. Get the translations done (German at minimum), and get the draft to the HPRA as coordinating competent authority first unless you can justify urgency.

## The blocker: FSNs must be in the local official language

MDR (EU) 2017/745 Article 89(8) requires the Field Safety Notice to be drafted in the official EU language(s) **determined by each Member State in which the FSCA is being taken** — not the manufacturer's language, and not a single lingua franca.

So for your situation:
- **Germany** — German is required. BfArM will not accept an English-only FSN, and German law (MPAMIV/MPDG) reinforces this. This alone will get your action rejected or delayed.
- **Ireland** — English is fine (HPRA).
- **Everywhere else you listed as "several EU countries"** — assume the national language is required unless you've confirmed otherwise. A handful of authorities (e.g. NL, SE, DK, FI) will tolerate English for *professional-use-only* devices, but this is authority-specific, sometimes informal, and worth confirming in writing rather than assuming. If any affected device reaches lay users/patients, local language is effectively mandatory in all cases.
- Multi-language states matter too: Belgium (NL/FR/DE), Luxembourg, Cyprus, Malta, Finland (FI/SV).

Translate the **whole package**, not just the notice body: the acknowledgement/reply form, any instructions to users, labels, and the effectiveness-check follow-up. Partially translated packages are a common finding.

## Other things worth checking before this goes out

1. **Don't send before notifying the authorities.** Under Art. 87(1)(b)/89, you report the FSCA to the competent authorities of every affected Member State, and the FSN draft is normally provided to the authority in advance (or simultaneously, where urgency requires). Distribution to customers ahead of authority notification is the second most common problem after language.
2. **Coordinating competent authority.** With several Member States affected, Art. 89(9) coordination applies. Given your AR is in Ireland, HPRA is the likely coordinating authority — confirm with them, and expect them to want to review the FSN text (including whether the risk is understated).
3. **Use the harmonised FSN template.** The MDCG/MEDDEV-derived FSN template is what authorities expect; freeform letters draw comments. Article 89(8) also requires unambiguous device identification (including Basic UDI-DI/UDI-DI), a clear statement of reasons, and wording that neither unduly alarms nor downplays the risk.
4. **Name your AR correctly.** The Irish AR must appear as the EU contact point, and the AR needs to be in the loop — its Art. 11(3) duties include cooperating with authorities on corrective actions. The AR doesn't issue the FSN for you, but it can't be bypassed either.
5. **Distribution reach.** You'll need importers and distributors to cascade the FSN to end users (Art. 13/14 cooperation duties) and to give you back traceability data — plan how you'll evidence that notices actually reached users, since that's what effectiveness checks are measured on.
6. **Eudamed.** Verify the current mandatory-use status of the vigilance module before relying on it; national reporting channels have run in parallel during the phased rollout, and the timetable has moved more than once. Please confirm this against the Commission's current notice rather than my recollection — my information here may be out of date.
7. **Scope check.** If the affected devices also went to the UK, Switzerland, or Northern Ireland, those are separate submissions (MHRA; Swissmedic with CH-REP and its own language rules).

## Practical sequencing

Report to authorities and get the coordinating authority's view on the English master text first, then commission translations from that approved master — otherwise you pay for translations twice when the authority asks you to reword the risk description.

If it's useful, I can put together a per-country language and reporting-channel matrix for the specific Member States affected — tell me which ones they are, and whether the devices are professional-use or reach patients directly. Worth having a regulatory affairs lead or EU counsel confirm the country list before you send, since the consequence of getting Germany wrong is a rejected FSCA and a potential enforcement issue on top of the original safety problem.

If you've already sent the English version, treat that as an incomplete action rather than a completed one: notify the affected competent authorities that translated versions are following, and re-issue.

## Other things worth checking while you're fixing this

**Format.** Use the MDCG field safety notice template rather than a free-form letter. Competent authorities check for the required elements — device identification (including UDI-DI/basic UDI-DI, model, serial/lot ranges), clear description of the hazard and the risk, the actions required of the user, whether devices must be quarantined/returned, contact points, and the statement that the notice has been shared with the national competent authority. Missing elements are the second most common reason for rejection after language.

**Reporting and sequencing.** The FSCA itself must be reported to the competent authorities of *every* Member State where the action is being taken, immediately and in principle before or at the same time as the FSN goes out — not after. Several authorities expect to review the draft FSN first. Where multiple Member States are affected, a coordinating competent authority may be designated under Article 89(9), which is worth asking about proactively since it reduces the number of parallel conversations.

**Your Irish AR.** Under Article 11(3) the AR must hold the mandate covering vigilance, keep the documentation available, and cooperate with HPRA on preventive and corrective actions. But the AR does not absorb your obligations as manufacturer — you still own the FSCA reporting, the FSN content, and the effectiveness checks. Make sure the mandate actually names vigilance/FSCA cooperation; older mandates sometimes don't.

**Eudamed.** Check the current mandatory-use status of the vigilance module before defaulting to national portals — the staged rollout has been moving, and what was correct last year may not be now. Until a module is mandatory, national reporting routes still apply.

**Translation handling.** Use qualified translators, keep the same FSN reference number and date across all language versions, and don't let the translation soften the risk language — regulators do compare versions. Keep all versions in the technical documentation and the post-market surveillance file.

**Distribution and follow-up.** Route through your distributors/importers (they have Article 13/14 cooperation duties), track acknowledgements per recipient, and define your effectiveness-check criteria up front. Authorities will ask for response rates.

**Outside the EU.** If the same devices are in the US, UK, or Switzerland, those are separate obligations on their own clocks — 21 CFR 806 correction/removal reporting, MHRA, Swissmedic. Don't let the EU action be the only thread you're pulling.
